title: The months have themes
hookLine: January the Holy Name, March Joseph, May Mary, June the Sacred Heart, October the rosary, November the dead

cards: In some Catholic homes, May means fresh flowers in front of a statue of Mary, and November means a list of the family's dead tucked beside the candles.
Under the feasts walked all year, from Advent to Christ the King, there's a second, quieter calendar. Not days. Months.
Each month has its own devotion, and where families keep them, they shape what's on the shelf and what's prayed at night.

teach.b: First, what this isn't. The month themes aren't part of the official liturgical calendar. No rule requires them; the Mass doesn't change because it's May.
They're popular devotions, encouraged by popes, and customs vary from country to country. Here's the common pattern.
January, the Holy Name of Jesus, the name given at his circumcision on the eighth day after Christmas. March, Saint Joseph, whose feast falls on the nineteenth.
May, Mary: flowers before her statue, and in some parishes a May crowning, where a child sets a wreath on Mary's head.
June, the Sacred Heart, since its feast usually falls then. July, often the Precious Blood. October, the rosary, the month of the feast of Our Lady of the Rosary on the seventh.
November, the holy souls, the dead, opening with All Saints and All Souls. Look at what the months are doing. They follow the feasts, and stretch a single day into a season of attention.
And they map onto ordinary life: Mary in spring flowers, the dead as the leaves come down in the north.
A line from Ecclesiastes, in the Douay-Rheims, fits the whole idea: "All things have their season, and in their times all things pass under heaven." A month is long enough to form a habit.
The feast is the door; the month is the room behind it.

how: Many Catholics follow traditional monthly devotions, such as May for Mary with May crownings, June for the Sacred Heart, October for the rosary and November for the dead; these are popular customs, not part of the official liturgical calendar.

games.q: it's May, and a parish child asks if the Mass will be different because it's Mary's month. what's the honest answer?
o: yes, every Mass in May is a Mary Mass.
no; the month themes are devotions, not liturgical rules.
games.why: the Mass follows the liturgical calendar. the month's theme lives in devotions: flowers, May crownings, prayers at home.

practice: What month is it right now, and which of today's themes belongs to it, or the nearest one? Picture one small sign of it: a flower for May, a picture for June, beads by the bed for October, a list of names for November.
If you pray, offer the month; if you don't, simply notice the season you're in.

wordCard.voice: May crowning. The parish custom in May when a child sets a wreath on a statue of Mary's head, one of the devotions behind the month's themes. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: every month a door. Whatever month it is, one stands open. Day six hundred eighty-nine.
